answers.answer: CAP describes computers communicating over a network, including separate servers holding copies of the same data. Copies hold local values and need messages to learn changes made elsewhere. If a network split prevents communication, the system cannot guarantee both CAP consistency and CAP availability. Choosing any two letters at all times is misleading: the conflict is conditional on a partition, and outside partitions CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability. A partition prevents parts of the system exchanging messages; it does not mean all servers crashed. Both sides can still run and receive client requests. Partition tolerance means accounting for communication failures, not promising all operations stay available. Ignoring partitions in discussion cannot repair the connections needed to share changes; adding servers cannot remove that dependence.

evidence.quote: When a network split prevents communication, a system cannot guarantee both the latest data and successful completion of every request.
Prevents parts of a system from exchanging messages. Servers on both sides can still be running and receiving requests.
Means the design accounts for these communication failures. It does not promise that every operation remains available.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability.

answers.answer: CAP consistency is linearizability: operations fit one valid single-copy order respecting real time. If a write completes before a read starts and there is no intervening write, that read must reflect the completed write. Overlapping operations may be ordered either way if the resulting single-copy order is valid; no globally synchronized timestamp on every request is required. Eventual convergence permits temporarily old copies; ACID consistency instead preserves defined database rules. CAP availability requires every valid request reaching a working server eventually to get a successful result, including data for a read. It has no requirement for instantaneous completion or a practical latency target. Refusing the affected operation or returning an error does not successfully perform it and therefore sacrifices availability, even if it avoids stale data. An uptime percentage measures something different from eventual successful completion of every such request.

evidence.quote: If a write completes before a read begins, and no intervening write changes the value, the read must reflect that write.
Overlapping operations may be placed in either order, provided the resulting order is valid for one copy.
This differs from eventual convergence and from ACID consistency, which concerns preserving defined database rules.
Means every valid request that reaches a working server eventually gets a successful result.
CAP availability does not mean fast, immediately answered, or a particular uptime percentage. The theorem requires eventual per-request completion and sets no practical response-time target.
An error response is not successful completion of the requested operation.

answers.answer: B knows its initial local value 0 but cannot learn which write completed at A across the broken connection. Since the write of 1 completed before the read began and no other write occurred, consistency requires the read to return 1. Returning 0 completes the read but violates consistency. Refusing it or waiting indefinitely avoids an old answer but fails eventual successful completion, so availability is not guaranteed. Guessing 1 happens to match this particular write but cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes: B has no delivered information distinguishing 1 from a different written value.

evidence.quote: If a write completes before a read begins, and no intervening write changes the value, the read must reflect that write.
B cannot know about a change that no message can deliver.
The read succeeds, but breaks consistency.
B avoids returning old data, but cannot guarantee availability.
Guessing the new value cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes.

answers.answer: To preserve consistency, allow only operations that can safely fit the required single order, and make unsafe reads or writes wait or fail. Otherwise an unseen completed write could make an answered read old or an independently accepted write incompatible with the agreed history. This need not stop everything: in the supplied three-server majority agreement example the connected pair can commit writes, while the isolated server cannot commit alone. To preserve availability, separated live nodes keep completing requests using their local information, giving up the guarantee that later reads reflect earlier completed writes across the system. A stale read observes an older copy; conflicting accepted writes are different changes to the same item independently accepted on different sides. Recovery requires exchanging changes and a policy to merge them, select one, or ask someone to resolve disagreement. Continued service does not ensure all update intentions survive: choosing one conflicting value can discard another intent. Cross-record rules also need their own protection.

evidence.quote: Preserves consistency during a partition. Some requests must wait or fail.
If the network splits into two servers and one, the connected pair can continue committing writes. The isolated server cannot commit writes on its own.
Safely coordinated operations can continue; favoring consistency need not shut down every part of the system.
Reads can return older data. If both sides accept writes, they can produce conflicting changes to the same item.
After communication returns, the system exchanges changes. It needs a rule to merge them, select one, or ask someone to resolve the conflict.
Availability supplies no automatic safe merge. Selecting one conflicting value can lose another user's intent, and cross-record rules require their own protection.

answers.answer: Eventual consistency means copies converge on a resulting state if new updates stop, communication resumes, and required updates and reconciliation reach every copy. It specifies no fixed catch-up deadline or immediate read-your-writes guarantee, and agreement on the result does not ensure every concurrent intent survives. The merge, selection, or human-resolution policy determines which changes survive. An operation requiring a read never to be older than a completed write must preserve the single-copy real-time order: during a split it can proceed only when safe, otherwise clients must wait or receive failure. After recovery, operations can resume when coordinated safely and reads still must reflect completed writes; reconciliation cannot simply excuse an earlier stale answer. An operation permitting temporarily old results can keep answering on live reachable nodes using local copies during the split. Clients can see staleness, and if both sides accept writes they can encounter conflicts. After recovery changes must be exchanged and reconciled, for example keeping an offline edit pending until a person resolves conflicting edits; eventual convergence requires the stated conditions. Guarantees should be chosen per operation and its selected read behavior, since a database can offer different read guarantees. Permanently labeling a whole vendor would hide these different choices. The lesson supplies no vendor-specific configuration details. CAP alone does not determine normal-operation latency, capacity, or cost; those require separate evaluation.

evidence.quote: Copies converge if new updates stop, communication resumes and the required updates and reconciliation reach every copy.
Convergence means agreement on a resulting state. It does not promise that every conflicting edit survives; the conflict-resolution policy determines the result.
Eventually gives no fixed deadline or immediate read-your-writes guarantee.
A database can offer different read guarantees. Choose for the operation rather than assuming every request has the same behavior.
Safely coordinated operations can continue; favoring consistency need not shut down every part of the system.
Can remain pending until conflicting changes are resolved.
It does not predict normal-operation latency, capacity or operating cost; evaluate those separately.
